lines.text: Bear's Notes One Electron Interferes With Itself
Fire electrons at two slits so slowly that only
one is ever in the machine — each arrives
as a single dot.
Ten electrons in, the dots look like random specks
— no pattern at all.
Common sense says they should pile into two heaps,
one behind each slit.
Keep firing, and something impossible begins to show.
Ripples passing through two openings overlap — crest on
crest brightens, crest on trough cancels.
So a wave hitting two slits paints stripes on
the far screen:
strong, weak, strong.
A ball can't overlap with anything:
it takes one slit or the other.
Balls through two slits stack into exactly two heaps
— nothing in between, no stripes.
Now watch the real electrons:
two hundred dots, and a faint clustering appears.
Six thousand dots, and unmistakable stripes are forming.
Seventy thousand dots:
clean bright and dark bands — a full interference
pattern.
Lay the wave's stripe pattern over the dots, and
it fits perfectly.
And there are bands where electrons never land —
forbidden zones no two-heap story can explain.
Remember:
the electrons flew alone — there was never a
second electron to interfere with.
So each electron's wave passes through both slits at
once and interferes with itself.
The dot is just where the electron is found;
the stripes map where finding it is likely.
That likelihood map has a name:
psi squared, the square of the electron's wave function.
And the stripe spacing is set by the electron's
wavelength — lambda equals h over p, de Broglie's
rule.
One electron arrives like a particle and travels like
a wave — both, every single time.
Peek at which slit it took, and the stripes
vanish — not because you jostled it, but because
you know.
This isn't just electrons:
molecules of two thousand atoms have painted the same
stripes.
You have a wavelength too — walking, about ten
to the minus thirty-five meters, far too small for
any doorway to reveal.
We didn't say what the wave function actually is,
or how crystals first revealed matter waves — each
is its own video.
Try it yourself:
compute your own de Broglie wavelength, h over m
times v, on your next walk.
Thanks for watching One Electron Interferes With Itself —
more at youtube dot com, slash, at Nik Bear
Brown.
